title: YOU NEVER TOUCHED THEM—SO WHY DID JESUS CALL IT ADULTERY?
paragraphs:
YOU NEVER TOUCHED THEM—SO WHY DID JESUS CALL IT ADULTERY?
What Jesus Meant When He Said Lust Can Begin in the Heart—and Why His Terrifying Words Were Never Meant to Leave the Guilty Without Hope
There are sins nobody sees.
No hotel room.
No secret apartment.
No physical affair.
No incriminating message your spouse accidentally discovers.
No church scandal.
No public confession.
Nothing anyone could screenshot and send around.

You can sit in church with your Bible open, sing about holiness, hug your family afterward, shake the pastor’s hand, post a Scripture verse before bed—and still carry a private world inside you that nobody knows exists.
Except Jesus.
And perhaps that is why His words in the Sermon on the Mount can feel so frighteningly personal.
Jesus said:
“Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη· Οὐ μοιχεύσεις.”
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’”
Then He went deeper.
“ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:27–28.
Read those words slowly.
Because Jesus just walked past the locked door.
Past the browser history.
Past the outward reputation.
Past the carefully managed Christian image.
Straight into the heart.
And suddenly the question is no longer merely:
“Have I ever physically committed adultery?”
The question becomes:
“What have I been allowing my heart to do when nobody is watching?”
That question changes everything.
But before shame takes this passage somewhere Jesus did not take it, something important needs to be understood.
Jesus was not saying that noticing that another human being is physically attractive is automatically adultery.
He was not declaring that every involuntary thought, temptation, or momentary awareness makes someone guilty of the completed sin He describes.
The Greek wording matters.
Matthew records:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
The word translated “looking” comes from βλέπω—blepō.
But the force of the sentence does not rest on seeing alone.
The crucial expression is:
“πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι”
pros to epithymēsai.
It expresses looking directed toward desire—looking with the purpose of lusting.
That is different from simply possessing eyes.
Different from recognizing beauty.
Different from temptation arriving unexpectedly.

Jesus is exposing something deeper: the deliberate gaze that welcomes lust, feeds it, returns to it, imagines, consumes, and inwardly turns another person into the object of sexual desire outside the holiness God intended.
Temptation may knock.
Jesus is talking about opening the door, pulling up a chair, and feeding it dinner.
And some people reading this know exactly what that means.
Because sometimes the first look really was accidental.
But the second wasn't.
Sometimes the image appeared unexpectedly.
But going back wasn't accidental.
Sometimes the thought entered without permission.
But keeping it alive became a choice.
Sometimes you told yourself:
“I would never actually do anything.”
And perhaps you haven't.
But Jesus refuses to let physical restraint become camouflage for inward surrender.
Because Jesus does not merely want faithful bodies.
He wants faithful hearts.
The word Matthew uses is καρδίᾳ—kardia.
Heart.
In biblical thought, the heart is not merely the place of romantic emotion. It describes the inner person—the realm of desire, intention, thought, will, and moral direction.
Jesus is saying something devastatingly simple:
Sin does not suddenly become serious when somebody catches you.
It was already serious when your heart began making peace with it.
That is uncomfortable because human beings are remarkably skilled at measuring righteousness by comparison.
“At least I never cheated.”
“At least I never slept with anyone.”
“At least nobody got hurt.”
“At least my spouse doesn't know.”
“At least it's only pornography.”
“At least it's only fantasy.”
“At least it's only looking.”
“At least it's only in my mind.”
And Jesus quietly removes the words “at least.”
Because the kingdom of God is not built upon learning how close we can stand to darkness without technically stepping into it.
Jesus wants the heart.
All of it.
The hidden room too.
Especially the hidden room.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading needs to stop pretending.
Maybe nobody knows what happens after midnight.
Maybe nobody knows what you erase.
Maybe your spouse thinks everything is fine.
Maybe your parents think you're fine.
Maybe the people at church think you're strong.
Maybe you are the person others ask for spiritual advice.
Yet there is a private battle behind the screen.
Pornography.
Fantasy.
Secret messages.
Replaying someone's body in your imagination.
Following accounts you know awaken something destructive.
Returning to pictures you know you should leave alone.
Emotionally feeding an attraction toward someone who does not belong to you.
Looking longer because something inside you wants more.
And afterward comes the familiar silence.
Delete.
Close.
Clear history.
Put the phone down.
Promise God again.
“Never again.”
Then morning comes.
Life continues.
Nobody knows.
But you know.
And God knows.
This is where many people make another dangerous mistake.
They hear Jesus exposing their sin and assume He is pushing them away.
But look at who is speaking.
This is Jesus Christ.
The One who exposes darkness because He came to rescue people from darkness.
The One who tells the truth about sin because lies cannot heal us.
The One who refuses to rename bondage “freedom” simply to protect our feelings.
Jesus does not expose the wound because He enjoys watching us bleed.
The Great Physician exposes the wound because hidden wounds cannot be treated while we insist they aren't there.
That is why the next words of Jesus sound so severe.
“If your right eye causes you to sin…”
The Greek says:
“εἰ δὲ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου ὁ δεξιὸς σκανδαλίζει σε…”
And Jesus continues with shocking imagery about tearing it out and throwing it away. Then He says essentially the same concerning the right hand.
Matthew 5:29–30.
Jesus is using deliberately radical language to communicate the deadly seriousness of sin.
The answer is not literal self-mutilation.
Removing an eye cannot remove lust from the heart.
A blind person can still lust.
Removing a hand cannot regenerate the soul.
Jesus has already identified the battlefield.
The heart.
His language demands ruthless repentance.
Whatever continually feeds the sin must stop being treated as harmless.
That might mean deleting an app.
Ending a secret conversation.
Unfollowing an account.
Installing accountability software.
Moving the phone out of the bedroom.
Confessing to a mature believer.
Ending access to something you repeatedly use for sin.
Walking away from a relationship that survives on secrecy.
Changing routines.
Stopping the excuses.
Not because these actions purchase forgiveness.
They don't.
Not because discipline saves you.
It cannot.
But genuine repentance does not keep building comfortable furniture inside the room it claims to be leaving.
Jesus takes sin seriously because sin destroys what God loves.
Lust teaches us to consume people who bear God's image.
It separates bodies from souls.
It trains the imagination to ask, “What can this person give me?” instead of, “How should this person be honored before God?”
It can slowly teach husbands to compare their wives with fantasies no real woman was created to satisfy.
It can teach wives to emotionally or sexually fantasize about someone other than the covenant partner beside them.
It can train single people to rehearse intimacy without covenant, sacrifice, responsibility, or love.
And pornography magnifies the deception by turning someone's body into content.
Swipe.
Watch.
Consume.
Close.
Find another.
But there is a human being on that screen.
A person made in the image of God.
A person with a childhood.
A person with wounds you cannot see.
A person Jesus commands you not merely to avoid touching unlawfully, but to learn to see differently.
Christian purity is not pretending bodies aren't beautiful.
It is learning to see human beings as more than bodies.
It is recovering holy vision.
And if this article is hurting right now, please keep reading.
Because conviction is not the end of this story.
The Gospel is.
Maybe you've already failed.
Maybe repeatedly.
Maybe you stopped counting years ago.
Maybe pornography has followed you from adolescence into marriage.
Maybe you committed actual adultery.
Maybe your marriage shattered because of what you did.
Maybe someone trusted you and you betrayed them.
Maybe you were exposed publicly.
Maybe your scandal has a name.
Maybe yours has never left the heart.
Either way, Christianity does not begin with good people congratulating themselves for being cleaner than everybody else.
It begins with sinners who need a Savior.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not lower God's standard until our sin becomes acceptable.
He does something infinitely more costly.
He bears the judgment sinners deserve.
The same Jesus who preached Matthew 5 would eventually walk toward a cross.
He would be stripped.
Mocked.
Shamed.
Crucified.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Because sin was so serious that redemption would cost blood.
And because His love was so great that He willingly gave His life.
At the cross, holiness and mercy are not enemies.
They meet.
Christ died for sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And therefore the person trapped in lust does not have to choose between pretending to be innocent and drowning forever in condemnation.
There is another way.
Confession.
Repentance.
Faith.
Grace.
Transformation.
Jesus.
The Gospel does not say:
“Clean yourself up enough and maybe Christ will receive you.”
The Gospel announces that sinners can come to Christ because Christ is the Savior sinners desperately need.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace actually makes real repentance possible.
You stop defending what Jesus died to free you from.
You bring the hidden thing into His light.
You call sin what God calls it.
You ask forgiveness.
You turn.
And when you stumble, you do not turn your failure into permission to surrender.
You run back to Christ.
Again.
Not casually.
Not cheaply.
Not treating grace as a license.
But believing that the blood of Jesus is stronger than the shame telling you to hide.
There is a difference between a believer battling sin and a person making peace with sin.
Battle means there may be scars.
Battle means sometimes you crawl.
Battle means sometimes you need another Christian beside you.
Battle means confession may be humiliating.
Battle means boundaries may feel inconvenient.
Battle means you stop asking, “How much can I get away with?”
And begin asking:
“What must I remove because Jesus is worth more?”
Somebody needs that question tonight.
Not:
“How close can I get?”
But:
“How free do I actually want to become?”
Because perhaps the deepest tragedy of lust is not simply that it makes us desire something forbidden.
It can make us forget that Christ Himself is better.
Better than the image.
Better than the fantasy.
Better than five minutes of secret pleasure followed by another night of shame.
Better than the person you've been imagining.
Better than the affair.
Better than the hidden account.
Better than the version of yourself you keep feeding in darkness.
Jesus is better.
And purity is not God withholding happiness from you.
Purity is God teaching your desires that they were created for something holier than consumption.
So tonight, perhaps repentance begins quietly.
Maybe nobody applauds.
Maybe there is no dramatic music.
Maybe it is simply you sitting alone with God and finally refusing to lie.
“Jesus… this has owned part of me.”
“This is what I've been watching.”
“This is who I've been fantasizing about.”
“This is what I've been hiding.”
“I cannot keep calling slavery freedom.”
“Forgive me.”
“Clean me.”
“Teach me to see people differently.”
“Give me a heart that wants You more than this.”
And then get up and make repentance practical.
Delete what needs deleting.
End what needs ending.
Confess what needs confessing.
Seek mature Christian accountability.

If your sexual behavior has become compulsive and you repeatedly cannot stop despite serious consequences, seeking help from a qualified Christian counselor or other appropriate professional is not spiritual defeat. Wisdom does not compete with prayer.
Bring the darkness into light.
Because the enemy loves secrecy.
Christ calls people into truth.
And hear this carefully:
Your worst sexual sin does not have to become the final sentence of your life.
Peter's denial was not his final chapter.
The Samaritan woman's broken relational history was not the end of her story.

The sexually immoral in Corinth were not told that transformation was impossible; Paul reminded believers that some of them had once lived in grievous sins, but had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
The Gospel specializes in impossible rewrites.
That is why we keep saying it:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by making sin respectable.

He rewrites everything by forgiving sinners, cleansing the guilty, transforming hearts, restoring what can be restored, teaching His people holiness, and giving new identities to people who thought their worst chapter had already named them forever.
Maybe your scandal happened with another person.
Maybe yours happened behind a locked screen.
Maybe yours happened entirely inside your imagination.
Jesus still sees the heart.
And Jesus still saves sinners who come to Him.
So be honest.
Did this expose something you have been hiding?
You don't need to describe the details publicly.
But you can stop hiding spiritually.
Your testimony may become the sentence somebody else desperately needed to read tonight.
And please don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It never could.
Christ alone saves, by grace, received through faith.
But if you want your digital life to glorify God, one practical way is to use the reach He has placed in your hands to put biblical truth in front of someone who may never walk through a church door.
There may be a husband silently losing a battle nobody knows about.
A wife carrying betrayal she cannot explain.
A teenager learning sexuality from pornography.
A believer convinced God could never want them again.
A friend smiling publicly while privately drowning.
Supporting Gospel work is not a substitute for supporting your local church, caring for your family, helping the needy, or practicing generosity wherever God calls you.
But if this ministry has genuinely served you and you want to help it reach more people, your support allows you to participate practically in that mission.
Go to Jesus.
The point was never to make you stare endlessly at your dirt.
The point was to make you see your need for the Savior.
The Savior who sees the browser history.
The Savior who sees the fantasy.
The Savior who sees the second look.
The Savior who sees the affair.
The Savior who sees the tears afterward.
The Savior who sees the years of hiding.
And still calls sinners to come into the light.
Not so they can remain what they were.
So He can transform them.
Perhaps you came to this article wondering whether a hidden look could really matter that much.
Now you know why Jesus went after the heart.
Because long before sin becomes a scandal people can see, it often becomes a secret the heart has learned to protect.
And grace begins when you stop protecting what is destroying you.
Remember this when temptation whispers your name again:
Jesus did not expose your hidden room so you would die inside it. He opened the door because He intends to lead you out.
